title: The task
subtitle: what the lander senses, does, and is scored on

transcript.text: Lesson one. Before we evolve anything, let's look at the problem: what the lander senses, what it can do, and how it is scored.

This is Lunar Lander, from the Gymnasium library. The lander starts high above the surface, with a random push. The goal is to touch down softly between the two flags. At every step, the lander senses eight numbers. Its position, measured from the pad. Its horizontal and vertical speed. Its tilt, and how fast it is spinning. And two switches that say whether each leg touches the ground. And at every step, it must choose one of four actions. Do nothing, fire the left engine, fire the main engine, or fire the right engine. So whatever our network looks like, it has eight inputs and four outputs.

The game itself hands out points as it goes. Moving toward the pad, slowing down and staying level all earn points. Drifting away, speeding up and tilting cost them. There are also one-off events. Each leg that touches the ground earns ten points. Coming to rest earns a hundred. A crash, or flying off the screen, costs a hundred. And fuel isn't free. Every frame the main engine fires costs a little, and the side engines cost a tenth of that. So hovering forever is a losing strategy. Add it all up over one flight, and you get the episode's reward. An average of two hundred or more counts as solved. That reward is exactly what we will use as fitness.
Lesson two. The pilot is a neural network. But evolution never touches the network directly. It works on a genome, a recipe for building one.

Here is the network that evolution found, flying. The eight inputs come in on the left. Each connection multiplies a value by its weight. Orange connections are positive, blue ones are negative, and thicker means stronger. Each node adds up what comes in, and squashes it into a value between minus one and one. On the right are four scores, one per action. The action with the highest score fires. Watch the scores change from moment to moment as the lander flies. This network has no hidden nodes at all, just seventeen of the thirty-two possible connections. Nobody drew it. Its shape and every one of its weights came out of evolution. We will see why it stayed this small in the next lesson.

The genome is a list of genes. Node genes say which neurons exist. Connection genes say which two neurons are wired together, with what weight, and whether the connection is switched on. Read the list from top to bottom, and you can build the network on the right. Each connection gene also carries a historical marker, called its innovation number. It is handed out the first time that connection appears anywhere in the population, and every later copy keeps it. So if two genomes share a number, those genes have a common origin. This small idea is what makes crossover work, as we will see in lesson four. The library we use, neat-python, names each gene by the two nodes it connects, which does the same job.
Lesson three. NEAT starts every network as small as possible, and lets mutation make it bigger, one careful step at a time.

Each new genome starts as a copy of a parent, and then it mutates. There are three kinds of mutation. The most common one simply nudges a weight, or the bias of a node. In our setup, each weight has an eighty percent chance of a small nudge. Here, a positive connection drifts until it becomes negative. The second kind adds a connection, joining two nodes that were not connected before. It gets a new innovation number. Half of all new genomes get one of these. The third kind adds a node. It picks a connection and splits it in two. The old gene is switched off, and two new genes take its place. The connection into the new node gets a weight of one, and the one out keeps the old weight. So the network behaves almost the same as before. The structure has grown, without breaking what already worked. Connections and nodes can also be deleted, so networks can shrink too.

So what happened in the real run? Here is the champion of each generation. Every run starts fully connected, with all eight inputs wired to all four outputs, and no hidden nodes. For its first hundred and sixty generations, evolution mostly removed connections. The winner, from generation one hundred and sixty-four, has no hidden nodes at all, and just seventeen of the thirty-two connections it started with. Later, the population grew much bigger networks, with fifteen or more hidden nodes. But those flew worse on unseen flights, not better. A bigger network is not automatically a better one, and that is exactly why NEAT starts small.
Lesson four. How do you combine two neural networks with different shapes? NEAT's answer is the innovation number.

Here are two parents. Because every gene has an innovation number, we can line their genes up by number, even though the networks look different. Parent A is the fitter one. Genes that both parents have are called matching. A gene that one parent has in the middle of its list, where the other has a gap, is called disjoint. And a gene that comes after the other parent's last gene is called excess. The child takes each matching gene from either parent at random. The disjoint and excess genes come from the fitter parent. No matter how different the two parents look, the child is always a sensible network, because every gene keeps its place in history.

Crossover is one part of a generation. Let's put the whole loop together. First, evaluate: every one of the 150 genomes flies, and gets a fitness score. Then, speciate: sort the genomes into species of similar networks. That's the topic of the next lesson. Then, select: inside each species, the best twenty percent become parents, and the two very best are copied unchanged into the next generation. Finally, reproduce: crossover and mutation fill the population back up to 150. Then the loop starts again, a few hundred times.

title: Speciation
subtitle: protecting new ideas long enough to work

transcript.text: Lesson five. Speciation is the part of NEAT that gives new ideas time to work.

Here is the problem. A mutation that adds a node usually makes the network worse at first, because its new weights are not tuned yet. If every genome competed against every other one, that network would be thrown out right away, before it ever had a chance to improve. So NEAT measures how different two genomes are, using their genes. It counts the genes that don't match. It adds half of the weight differences of the genes that do match. And it divides the total by the size of the larger genome. Our library does this for the connections and for the nodes, and adds the two. If that distance is below two point two, the two genomes belong to the same species. Genomes then compete mostly inside their own species. Each species shares its offspring among its members, so a big species can't simply crowd out a small new one. And a species that stops improving for twenty generations is removed, so the population doesn't waste effort on dead ends.

This is the classic NEAT picture, from our run. Each band is one species, and its height shows how many of the 150 genomes belong to it. At the very start there is just one species, because every genome has the same shape. As mutations pile up, new species split off. They grow when they do well, and shrink and die when they stop improving. Over the whole run, twenty-seven species came and went.

title: Watching it evolve
subtitle: the real run, generation by generation

transcript.text: Lesson six. Now we watch the real training run, one generation at a time.

First, how do we score a genome? Its fitness is the average reward over five flights. Every genome in a generation flies the same starting positions, so the comparison is fair. The starting positions change each generation, so no genome can memorise one. But five flights are noisy, and the top genome is often just lucky. So each generation, its champion also flies a hundred flights that no genome ever trained on. We only call the problem solved when that unseen average reaches two hundred.

Every dot is one genome, and its color shows its species. In generation zero, every network is just the inputs wired straight to the outputs, with random weights. Almost all of them crash. Generation by generation, the cloud of dots creeps upward. Notice how wide it stays. Mutation keeps producing bad genomes too, and that variety is what evolution searches through. The green line is the champion on the hundred unseen flights. It first passes two hundred in generation thirty-seven. The best champion came from generation one hundred and sixty-four. On another hundred fresh flights, it lands ninety-five percent of the time. Late in the run the line sags, as the networks grow bigger without getting better.

Here is one whole generation flying together. All 150 genomes start from the same spot, and each flight is drawn as a trail. This is generation zero. At first, nearly every flight ends in a crash, or drifts off the screen. Fifty generations in, a few dozen trails curve down onto the pad. And late in the run, about a third of the population lands from this start, and their trails bundle together into one shared path. The rest still crash. Mutation keeps breaking things, and that is the price of searching.
Finally, here are the champions from different generations, all flying the same start. The early ones crash or drift away. Later champions slow down, straighten up, and land between the flags.
Lesson seven. Evolution built a network that lands. But what did it actually build? Let's take it apart.

One simple way to find out what matters is to switch a connection off, fly again, and see what breaks. Here is the winner flying, with all of its connections. The most important connection runs from the falling speed to the main engine, with a big negative weight. When the lander falls fast, its vertical speed is negative, so the main engine's score shoots up, and it brakes. Switch this one connection off, and the lander never lands at all. Next, the tilt angle feeds the left engine. This is the connection that keeps the lander upright. Without it, only five percent of flights land. And here is a surprise. Once the right leg touches the ground, its sensor tells the engines to stop, and votes for doing nothing. Without that, the lander keeps nudging itself and lands only fifteen percent of the time. Evolution ignored the left leg sensor completely. One leg was enough.

Here are the connections that matter most, ranked by how much the landing rate drops without them. Red bars mean the lander falls apart. Green bars mean it barely notices. Nine of the seventeen connections can go with almost no loss. A handful of them carry the whole skill. That's typical for evolved networks. They are not tidy, but the important parts are usually few, and you can find them.

Switching connections off shows what the network relies on. Watching where it fails shows what it is missing. On a thousand new flights, it landed ninety-seven percent of the time. Sixteen of its eighteen crashes ended to the right of the pad, where it tipped over on the slope. The other failures are stranger. Fourteen flights ran out of time, sitting on the pad. In eight of them, only the left leg was touching. Remember, the network ignores its left leg sensor. It waits for the right leg, and keeps nudging itself until the time runs out. And every failure began with a hard sideways push. A network with no hidden nodes handles the usual flight very well. These rare, hard starts are where a better network could still improve.
